description: Detect calls to printStackTrace() on Throwable or exception objects. The rule should flag code that directly prints a stack trace instead of using a logging framework.

Detect JUnit 5 test classes or JUnit 5 test methods that explicitly use public, protected, or private visibility. JUnit 5 tests should be package-private. Test methods are methods annotated with @Test, @RepeatedTest, @TestFactory, @TestTemplate, or @ParameterizedTest.

Detect direct printing to the console through System.out or System.err. Flag calls such as System.out.print, System.out.println, System.err.print, and System.err.println because production code should use a logger instead.

Detect uses of Charset.forName with standard charset names such as UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-16BE, UTF-16LE, US-ASCII, or ISO-8859-1. These should use the predefined constants in java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets instead.

Detect method or constructor parameters declared as array types where a varargs parameter would be clearer. Do not flag byte array parameters, and do not flag the String[] parameter of a public static void main method.

Detect constructors that do not explicitly call either super(...) or this(...). A constructor should start with an explicit call to the superclass constructor unless it delegates to another constructor in the same class.

Detect throw statements that directly create or throw raw exception types: RuntimeException, Throwable, Exception, or Error. Prefer throwing a more specific subclass that describes the actual failure.

Detect method or constructor declarations whose throws clause includes unchecked exception types. Unchecked exceptions such as RuntimeException subclasses should usually be documented with Javadoc rather than declared in the signature.

Detect static fields that are visible outside the declaring class and are not final. Non-private mutable static fields expose global mutable state and should instead be private, final, or immutable constants.
Detect boolean expressions that compare directly with true or false, such as x == true, x == false, x != true, or x != false. These comparisons are redundant and should be simplified.

Detect public methods or constructors with long parameter lists made mostly of simple values such as Strings. These APIs should usually group related parameters into a dedicated object instead of passing many separate values.
Detect methods with an empty body when the empty body has no explanatory comment. An empty method body should contain a comment if the emptiness is intentional.
Detect fields whose name is the same as a method name declared in the same class. A field and a method with the same name can make the API confusing because data and behavior are named identically.

Detect fields whose name matches the name of the class or interface that declares them. A field should not have the same name as its enclosing type because this is confusing and usually indicates poor naming.
Detect classes that implement Serializable but do not declare a serialVersionUID field. Each serializable class, including abstract serializable base classes, should define its own serialVersionUID.
Detect uses of java.util.Calendar. Code should prefer the modern java.time API, such as LocalDate, LocalDateTime, or ZonedDateTime, instead of the mutable and error-prone Calendar API.
Detect uses of java.util.Date. Code should prefer java.time types such as LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, Instant, or ZonedDateTime instead of the mutable and outdated Date API.

Detect methods that return null from a method whose return type is an array, Collection, Map, or another collection-like type. Such methods should return an empty collection or empty array instead of null.
Detect construction of SimpleDateFormat without an explicit Locale argument. SimpleDateFormat should be created with a Locale so formatting and parsing are not dependent on the JVM default locale.

Detect JUnit assertions that use constant boolean literals, such as assertTrue(true), assertTrue(false), assertFalse(true), or assertFalse(false). These assertions are redundant or should be replaced with fail() or normal control flow.
Detect string comparisons that use == or !=. String values should be compared with equals() or equalsIgnoreCase(), not with reference equality operators.
Detect calls to String.toLowerCase() or String.toUpperCase() that do not pass an explicit Locale. Case conversion should specify a locale to avoid behavior depending on the system default locale.
Detect calls to getClassLoader() that should use Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader() instead. In J2EE-style environments, the context class loader is usually the correct loader to use.

Detect code that creates or starts its own threads in J2EE or managed-server code. Applications should not directly create Thread objects or unmanaged thread pools because thread management belongs to the container.

Detect uses of Hashtable or synchronized Map wrappers where ConcurrentHashMap should be preferred for concurrent map access. Modern code should use java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap for efficient thread-safe maps.

Detect creation of java.util.Calendar instances only to obtain the current date or time. Calendar is heavyweight; prefer new Date() or java.time now() methods unless calendar-specific calculations are needed.

Detect direct use of FileInputStream, FileOutputStream, FileReader, or FileWriter constructors. Prefer java.nio.file.Files factory methods such as Files.newInputStream, Files.newOutputStream, Files.newBufferedReader, or Files.newBufferedWriter.
Detect calls to toString() on expressions that are already known to have type String. Calling toString() on a String is unnecessary and should be removed.
